newsitem.title: UK: Dlr seen heading up amid Germn credit speculation.
newsitem.headline: Dlr seen heading up amid Germn credit speculation.

text.p: The dollar's consolidation around 1.85 marks gives the Bundesbank ammunition to keep rates on hold but forex traders are likely to push the U.S. currency higher as speculation about the timing of a German credit tightening intensifies, analysts said.

The dollar reacted to today's announcement of another fixed rate repo tender at 3.00 percent with an initial half pfennig burst higher but reversed its gains quickly. "It was quite shrewd of the Bundesbank to keep rates steady today," said Robin Marshall, chief economist at Chase in London. "They want to avoid the impression they are going to war with the market on interest rates and at the same time keep the uncertainty alive between now and the next council meeting." The Bundesbank's policy-making council meets again on August 21 after a four week summer recess. In the intervening period, the prospects of a German rate increase as well as the performance of U.S. asset markets will be the major factors dictating the dollar's movements.

Interest rate speculation had intensified when the Bundesbank - in a break with recent tradition - announced repos only for the first two weeks but held off on the announcement of conditions at which it would offer funds to the market in the remaining two weeks.
Talk of a credit tightening after five years of lower rates accelerated when the dollar continued its spurt higher against the battered mark to a near-eight year high just over 1.89 marks last week.
But a sharp fall in U.S. asset markets on Friday has since helped push the dollar lower. At 1115 GMT it was at 1.8610/20 marks.

So far, the weakness of the mark has sparked verbal rhetoric from the Bundesbank but not overt central bank intervention even though latest reserve data showed some signs that the Buba might have been discreetly in the market.
Over the last year, the mark has fallen around 25 percent against the dollar and more than 30 percent against sterling.
As forex traders have become increasingly convinced that German interest rates will rise, the timing of a possible rise has moved into focus.
Analysts said the Bundesbank is likely to wait for domestic inflationary news to allow the repo rate to edge higher rather than appear to be forced into a move by the forex market.
"Adjusting interest rates in order to influence the exchange rate is out of character for the Bundesbank," said Tim Fox, chief treasury economist at Standard Chartered.

Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing, known to be one of the most hawkish members of the central bank's council, sounded a warning bell on inflationary pressure last week when he said German prices were moving in the wrong direction.
Final July inflation data released on Tuesday showed an annual inflation rate of 1.9 percent, the highest level since June 1995 and up from 1.7 percent in June.
Analysts expect the August CPI rate to exceed the 2.0 percent threshold, the level regarded as acceptable by the Bundesbank.

Import prices will also be closely watched by the market as the weakness of the mark is likely to put them under upward pressure. The dollar/mark exchange rate is particularly relevant as a large proportion of Germany's imports is priced in dollars.

The close historical relationship between the dollar/mark exchange rate on the one hand and import and consumer prices on the other, explains the Bundesbank's recent preoccupation with the exchange rate, analysts said.
The next monthly import price data, due to be released later this month, is expected to show a sharp increase in the wake of the dollar's strong gains in July.

"But it is by no means guaranteed that a rise in the cost of imported goods and services will be passed on to consumer prices because retailers and wholesalers might be able to absorb some of the extra costs," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy in London.

This would not be unprecedented. A rise in import prices during 1983/85, again inspired by a rise in dollar/mark and against a backdrop of subdued consumer spending, had no discernible effect on consumer prices, he said.

M3 money supply growth, another indicator watched by the Bundesbank, is at 6.4 percent, within the central bank's target corridor of 3.5 to 6.5 percent. The backbone of the dollar rally remains intact - a robust U.S. economy coupled with low inflation and a nascent economic recovery in Germany burdened with high unemployment and subdued consumer spending.
As long as this scenario holds true the dollar is likely to push back up, possibly hitting 1.90 marks soon, traders said.

"The market was a bit long above 1.87 marks today but this is nothing but a corrective phase in an uptrend," said a senior trader at a German bank in London. "I still see it going to 1.90 in the next week or two."

Joe Prendergast, head of global foreign exchange research at CSFB in London, said there was a risk of a larger correction into the low 1.80s area before the next push higher. The near-term direction was likely to come from the performance of U.S. asset markets, he said.
